speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: GASPE-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ESTABLISHMENT OF PARK IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to announce today that an agreement has been reached between the federal government and the government of the province of Quebec to establish a national park on Forillon Peninsula.

subsubtopic: GASPE-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ESTABLISHMENT OF PARK IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear,

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: GASPE-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ESTABLISHMENT OF PARK IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
The discussions concerning the establishment of this national park go back to the signing of the Federal-Provincial Rural Development Agreement between Canada and Quebec, in May, 1968, which dealt with the development of the Lower St. Lawrence region of the Gaspe area and of the Iles-de-la-Madelaine.
Since my appointment as Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, I have stated on several occasions that I attach great importance to the establishment of a national park in the Gaspe area and that I would do everything in my power to bring it to fruition.
The Gaspe national park is the first national park in Quebec. It is also the twentieth national park in Canada.
The establishment of this park completes our transcontinential network of national parks and permits us to maintain intact an extremely picturesque corner of our country for the benefit of future generations.
Under the terms of the agreement reached between the two governments, the province of Quebec will place the site of the Gaspe park at the disposal of the government of Canada for a period of 99 years. The agreement states, as well, that the province of Quebec will have the right to regain possession at the end of 60 years on repayment of all federal capital expenditures incurred by
the federal government during the 60-year period.
In either case, the government of Quebec agrees that the land would be used for the purposes of a park and conservation in perpetuity. This arrangement is renewable by agreement of the two parties.
Finally, the agreement provides that the park will reflect the linguistic character of Canada, and in particular the French character of Quebec. It is essential that any national park located in Quebec should be in keeping with the very personality of Quebec. The development of the Gaspe national park is above all a victory for the inhabitants of the Gaspe area. The population of the Gaspe peninsula in the past year has consistently urged on both governments the creation of this park, which will undoubtedly contribute to the economic development of that area.
The agreement reached by the federal government with the province of Quebec to establish this park is unique. This agreement completes the national park system by providing at least one park in each province. I hope that the same spirit of co-operation which has resulted in this agreement will make it possible to create other national parks in Quebec within established policy.
The transfer of administration and control of the land required would be for a term in this instance, but a term of such length that we are satisfied that future generations will not reverse it if it is as successful as we believe it will be.
The people of Quebec have not hitherto enjoyed the benefits which come from taking part in the national parks system. It is my belief this park will be recognized by all the citizens of Quebec as a significant enhancement of the economic and social well-being of the province. It will become, I am convinced, a permanent part of Quebec and of Canada for the benefit not only of the present generation but of untold generations to come.

subsubtopic: GASPE-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ESTABLISHMENT OF PARK IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party, we welcome the agreement

May 21. 1969
National Parks
between the federal government and the province of Quebec for the establishment of a national park in the Gaspe area.
Of course, this is good news not only for the country but also for the people of Quebec, and I must say that under this agreement both parties keep their jurisdiction, and that Quebec keeps also jurisdiction over its territory. This is the result of the dialogue and the mutual understanding which we would like to see at all times between the federal government and the province of Quebec.
Obviously, as implied in the statement, because of its special character, Quebec is very often asking for some assurances in regard to the establishment of national parks or the distribution of jurisdictions between the federal government and the province.
Mr. Speaker, as a member for Quebec and on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party, I am glad that this agreement has been reached, as it will help, I am sure, to promote the economic expansion of Quebec and to reduce significantly unemployment in this part of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, we deplore however that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) attempted to interrupt the dialogue between provincial authorities. When he went to the Gaspe peninsula, he addressed the Chambers of Commerce and tried to provoke a reaction within the population against the Quebec government. I am happy to see that the minister reversed his attitude, and I feel it is that reversal of attitude which has resulted today in the conclusion of this agreement.
On behalf of my party, I congratulate the Minister on having understood the situation and the demands of Quebec, and on succeeding in reaching this agreement, which will be beneficial not only, as I said as while ago, to the citizens of the lower St. Lawrence region, but to all Quebecers as well.
I urge the minister to carry on his dialogue and to show an understanding mind with Quebec authorities, so as to be able, in the near future, to enter into other agreements for the development of national parks in Quebec.
I read in a Quebec newspaper during the weekend that the minister intended to develop about ten national parks in the province of Quebec. It was even said that it was his intention to develop one in my own riding, in the Saguenay area. If the minister needs my influence with the Quebec government for the

development of this park as soon as possible, I will be pleased to co-operate.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we welcome this agreement, and we congratulate, not only the minister concerned, but also the Quebec authorities who understood the problem and were able to negotiate.

subsubtopic: GASPE-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ESTABLISHMENT OF PARK IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for two reasons we listened with some pleasure to the announcement of the minister. We listened with pleasure first because this exhibits that element of co-operation between the federal government and a provincial government we hope will be extended to other provinces in respect of other matters and for other reasons. We listened also to his announcement with pleasure, because a national park is like any other park in that its existence is one thing which contributes to the aesthetics of our life in this nation.
Even though, as I understood the minister to say, this completes a chain of national parks, we hope it will not be the end of this national chain, but that there will be opportunities for greater co-operation and participation in respect of parks development. I must put in a plug for my own area. Because of the great interest which exists in that vast northwestern section of British Columbia, so far totally ignored by the federal government in matters such as this, we hope this co-operation will extend to that area.
I am sure we all appreciated the enthusiasm with which the minister made his announcement. I hope he has the same enthusiasm when he is dealing with people that he has displayed in dealing with things such as national parks. We looked forward in the hope that today would be the day he would make a policy declaration about Indian affairs, because this is something we have been awaiting for a long, long period of time.

subsubtopic: GASPE-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ESTABLISHMENT OF PARK IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we congratulate the minister on his statement regarding the new agreement which has just been reached. For the first time in Quebec-this was long overdue-a national park will be established.
During the year when the negotiations were being held, we felt there was a great deal of uncertainty and of hesitation, and on some occasions we felt that the statements made by both parties were jeopardizing the future of that park.
May 21. 1969

We are happy to see that statements from both parties have now come to an end. I would not want to blame the minister for statements which rather tended to impede negotiations and to create misunderstandings.
We are proud to realize that the federal government has at least succeeded in coming to terms with the Quebec government in order to establish our first national park in our province, it being the 20th in Canada. This means, therefore, that we, in Quebec, have certainly not been spoiled with regard to national parks.
I would like to remind the minister-as he already knows-that in Quebec, many sites could be developed into national parks. We hope that the decision made today, in cooperation with the Quebec government, will lead to further agreements, other negotiations, so that other parks will be established in Quebec, particularly in my area, where the question of developing another national park is being seriously considered at the present time. In Quebec, there are some very fine holiday resorts, and I know that the establishment of national parks would help attract more tourists, in short, develop the tourist industry everywhere in Canada. That industry has not been neglected, judging by the number of national parks that have been developed in other provinces. But it was time the minister realized the situation created in Quebec and concluded an agreement with the government of that province.
We are happy for the people of the Gaspe peninsula. This region is known to everyone in Canada from sea to sea. It offers special touristic attractions and we are happy to see that after having been neglected for so long, it will get a national park which will promote its development, both from the touristic and the economic point of view.

subtopic: DECISION TO DEFER REVISIONS IN RATES ON EAST COAST FERRY SERVICES

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: DECISION TO DEFER REVISIONS IN RATES ON EAST COAST FERRY SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time now there has been speculation in the house concerning possible rate revisions on the government ferries operating from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to Prince Edward Island, from Nova Scotia to Newfoundland and from Nova Scotia to the State of Maine. The matter of rates for different classes of traffic on the
East Coast Ferry Service Rates government ferries operated on the east coast has been very carefully studied both by the government and by Canadian National Railways who operate these ferries on behalf of the government. Consultations were also held with officials in the provinces concerned. These studies have shown that a revision in rates is necessary.
In any such revision, careful attention should be given to the individual characteristics of each type of traffic; such factors as whether the service was essential or nonessential to each class of user, the structure of competitive rates, the cost of handling different types of traffic and the cost of alternative routes should be examined. Therefore, while it is clear that some rate changes must be forthcoming on these ferry services, not all of which I hasten to add will be upward, before instituting such changes the government wants to be certain that what has been proposed is consistent with and reflects the new transportation policy currently being developed for the Atlantic provinces. For this reason it has been decided not to institute rate revisions on the east coast ferry services until such time as the new Atlantic provinces transportation policy has been worked out and the government has had the opportunity to examine the proposed rates in light of this new policy.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-196, to provide for the establishment of the Canada Disaster Fund.

subtopic: MEASURE TO DECIDE POINT AT WHICH FEDERAL FUNDS SHOULD BE AVAILABLE
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: MEASURE TO DECIDE POINT AT WHICH FEDERAL FUNDS SHOULD BE AVAILABLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill is intended to meet the problem of deciding at what point disaster losses are beyond the capacity of a province to deal with effectively, and the disaster essentially becomes national. The bill sets up a fund to which contributions can be made in advance by federal and provincial governments and by individuals, companies and institutions. The board of trustees each year determines in advance, in respect of each province, the provincial financial tolerance point above which losses are of national scope. Should a disaster occur in that province, the board contributes to the province out of the fund in respect of the losses above the tolerance point. This bill will ensure prompt and efficient assistance to those areas which qualify and will help to eliminate any future provincial-federal disputes over the sharing of costs.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

Mr. Speaker, last night I had discussed some of the legal arguments which had been made against the official languages bill and had come to the conclusion that the most important fact about them was not the character of the arguments-they were poor arguments in themselves-but the fact that they

had been made, which showed there is concern among some of the people in this country about the possible implications of this bill. At the hour of adjournment I was coming to the question of compulsion which had been raised earlier by the hon. member for Bran-don-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale). That hon. member said, and I quote from page 8869 of Hansard for yesterday:
I think the nub of the matter is that this legislation represents compulsion to many, and no one likes legislative compulsion.
I regret to say I cannot understand the reasoning of my hon. friend. In looking over his speech the only substantiation I find is his quotation of what the leader of the Creditiste party said, which I think rather inaccurately states what the official languages bill attempts to do.
There is, however, a much more extreme statement of what I take to be a similar point of view about compulsion. I refer to an expression of opinion by the Hon. Joseph T. Thorson, the former president of the Exchequer Court of Canada, a civil libertarian of note but, to judge from his recent public utterances, not a constitutionalist of distinction. In an article published in April of this year in Chitty's Law Journal entitled "Bilingualism in the Courts-Is it Justified?", Mr. Thorson writes, as found on page 113:
-an intensive attempt is now being made to create a dual English-French Canadian nationality in Canada and to force its acceptance on the people of Canada on the ground that it is essential to Canadian unity.
I fail to understand the reasoning behind this line of argument. In the official languages bill there is perhaps an inducement, and certainly an opportunity, to the people of this country to participate in another of the official languages, but the only compulsion exercised by the bill is a compulsion which is exercised on the government and agencies of the government. What there is in the bill is a kind of persuasion, and persuasion is surely of the very essence of the democratic process. Sometimes democratic governments find it necessary to use compulsion and the force of the law with the imposition of penalties, but this is not the case with this bill. At most, in this case there is an inducement, one which I believe the Canadian people will sincerely welcome.
The argument of the hon. Mr. Justice Thorson, to which I referred a moment ago, is on the same level with his other arguments in respect of the official languages bill. I refer to his own interpretation of section 133

of the British North America Act. Before going on to discuss this section I should like to draw its terms to the attention of hon. members. Section 133 of the British North America Act provides as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the Parliament of Canada and the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or In any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
It also provides that:
The acts of the Parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
In his most literal explanation of section 133 the hon. Mr. Justice Thorson said, and I quote from page 110 of the article to which I have referred:
-French is not an official language of Canada anywhere in Canada . . . except as specified in the section, the French language does not have any special status in Canada.
I believe that to be an accurate conclusion in respect of the meaning of section 133, but Mr. Justice Thorson went on to say:
It follows that any legislation either by Parliament or by the legislature of Ontario that would attempt to make French an official language or endow it with a status equal to English in an area where it is not now an official language or does not now have such a status would be in conflict with the provisions of section 133-
He further went on to say at page 112 of the same article:
It follows as a necessary consequence that, except as specified in the section, English is the only official language of Canada.
The statement that English is the official language of Canada is an extraordinary one. Nowhere in section 133 is it specified that English is the official language of Canada, and nowhere in the British North America Act is this so specified. Why should an inference be drawn from the silence of the statute that English is the official language of Canada when the section specifically deals with both the English and French languages and confers exactly the same rights and privileges upon both? How could English come to be the official language of Canada? Would it be by an act of the parliament of Canada? This is the very thing that the hon. Mr. Justice Thorson has contended cannot be done. Would it be done by an act of the legislature of the
May 21. 1969

province of Ontario or, indeed, by any provincial legislature or any combination of them? Certainly there is nothing either in our constitutional theory or history to warrant such a method of establishing an official language.
The fact is that there is no official language in Canada at present because the constitution of Canada does not establish an official language. Nor does Bill C-120 attempt to establish an official language. It does attempt to establish an official language for certain limited purposes under the jurisdiction of the federal government, but in constitutional law we have no official language. It is true, by reason of a predominance of English speaking people in our political life, and because to some extent of the facts of economic life in this country, that we have had a language which has the status of a predominant language. However, the Minister of Justice points out that some lawyers cannot handle either English or French.

speechtext:
The fact is that it is not in the constitution but in the living life of Canada that the future of the English and French languages in our country is to be determined. This bill is an attempt to influence these living practices of the people of Canada. It is an attempt at long last to give an opportunity to our French speaking citizens in the province of Quebec, and those spread throughout other provinces, to use their language in an official way in communication with the government and its agencies.
The bill itself is indeed a solution in law, but it is also a solution which will have an effect on the practices of the people. It gives us an opportunity which we have not had before, that is, to express bilingualism and, indeed, to begin to approach multilingualism. I believe that most people in the country
Official Languages
welcome this opportunity. It is for this reason I believe that the young people of Canada, the people who see the future most clearly, are the ones who are most enthusiastically behind this bill.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The Minister of Justice said yesterday that the young people of this country, English speaking and French speaking, are strongly in favour of this legislation. I know that this applies in my own heavily ethnic riding. The young people of Canada understand what is the future of the new world and of Canada as part of that world. If we pass this bill we will be honouring our past, fulfilling our present, and securing our future.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to support this bill because it is based upon the principle embodied in the British North America Act which guarantees the right to use both our official languages in any part of the country in which a sizeable minority resides. Recently Ontario and New Brunswick, which have large French speaking minorities, introduced legislation guaranteeing the use of the French language within their borders.
Last July there was unanimous approval in the Ontario legislature for a resolution establishing the right to address the house in either English or French. Premier Robarts announced that four task forces had been established to look into bilingualism in the courts, the provincial public service, municipal government and the publication of statutes and official publications of the house in both official languages. School legislation was adopted in Ontario providing for greater use of French as a teaching language in high schools and making the traditional use of French in some elementary schools a legal right. In the high schools a course must be taught in French if 20 or more students wish it.
In New Brunswick, a province with a 60 per cent English speaking majority, the legislature has unanimously passed a bill proclaiming official bilingualism at the provincial level.
Such legislation was acceptable to the English speaking majorities in those provinces largely because of the generous attitude taken by the province of Quebec toward its English speaking minority, even though no legislation guaranteeing the right to use the English language had been passed.

May 21. 1969
Official Languages
Last autumn Premier Bertrand of Quebec introduced Bill No. 85 which would guarantee English speaking rights by law. Shortly after its introduction, however, the bill was suddenly withdrawn, no substitute was introduced in its place and there is no indication that a suitable substitute will be introduced.
Many English speaking Canadians believe strongly that French speaking rights in their part of the country should not be guaranteed by law unless those living in the area where French is the predominant language, the province of Quebec, show an equal willingness to guarantee by law the rights of English speaking Canadians in that province.
If the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would leave his ivory tower in Ottawa and talk to people in all parts of the country, particularly those in western Canada, about this matter, he would be familiar with the very strong feeling which exists.
I am convinced that the purpose of a bill such as the one before us should be to promote national unity in all parts of our country. I am convinced that if this bill is passed before the province of Quebec passes a suitable substitute for Bill No. 85, which was withdrawn last autumn, it will contribute greatly to disunity in this country. I therefore urge the Prime Minister to confer with Premier Bertrand while this bill is being seriously considered in committee over the next few weeks, as I am sure it will be, and persuade him, in the interests of national unity, to reintroduce and pass without delay a suitable substitute for Bill No. 85, guaranteeing by law the rights of the English speaking minority in Quebec. This should be done before the bill comes back into the house for third reading and final passage. I am convinced that this is the only way people in all parts of the country-I underline "all parts of the country"- can be persuaded that this bill is a fair measure and should be accepted, thus making it possible for national unity, not disunity, to be promoted across our country.
I am also very strongly of the opinion that to pass the bill before people in all parts of the country are so convinced would not be in the national interest. Therefore I urge the Prime Minister to speak to Premier Bertrand about this matter. The Premier of Quebec is a very reasonable man who I am sure is anxious to see national unity in all parts of Canada. I believe he is just as interested in achieving national unity as we all are. After giving this matter considerable thought, and

after consultation with those in his government, I am sure Premier Bertrand will introduce-in the Quebec legislature a suitable substitute for Bill No. 85, and his government will pass it, thereby making it possible for French speaking rights to be guaranteed to those parts of the country which have French speaking minorities. This would make our country more truly bilingual and fair-minded in keeping with what the Fathers of Confederation had in mind when more than 100 years ago they passed the act of confederation.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal this afternoon with Bill C-120, an act respecting the status of the official languages of Canada.
Several members have already spoken in French. I have taken an immersion course on two occasions at the civil service school of languages. I come from Ottawa, Mr. Speaker, and I started long ago to learn French at school. Like all English-speaking citizens of the province of Ontario, I did not learn it too well.
I take this opportunity to thank the teachers of the civil service school of languages who were very competent. They have helped me a great deal to improve my French. I think other members should also avail themselves of this opportunity to improve their knowledge of the second official language of the country.

For the past two days, Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the debate on the official languages bill. One of the most striking features of that debate has been the nature of some of the speeches. Obviously, the basic principle of the bill touches a deep, emotional chord in many people. I think particularly of the speech made last week by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) and that made yesterday by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin), whom I see in the house at this time.
In many ways the debate recalls the election campaign in the constituency I have the honour to represent, Ottawa West. My Conservative opponent in the last federal election campaign, as in the previous three election campaigns in which we faced each other, took a position similar to that of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. He campaigned against a policy of bilingualism in the public service and against the principles
May 21, 1969

embodied in the official languages bill. I believed then, as I do now, that the official languages bill is an essential instrument of national unity which embodies one of the principles upon which we will re-establish our federal state.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in introducing this bill last October, attacked the concept of two nations and maintained that Canada had to survive as one national state. Within this state there is no room for special status, and there is no room for a degree of autonomy granted to any province that is not available to any other province. The federal power must speak for the French language minority outside Quebec as well as for the English language minority within Quebec. In order to secure these rights, it may well be necessary to embody them in constitutional amendments.
In this House of Commons there can be only one class of member. There cannot be a member elected in any part of Canada who does not have a right to legislate, to vote on the matters that come before us, and to make decisions involving the national interest, equal to the rights enjoyed by every other member. There cannot be members elected from the province of Quebec who would make decisions affecting areas outside that province which they cannot make for the province in which they were elected. It follows in a most logical fashion that if we are to maintain the House of Commons in the style we have known, with members elected from all regions having equal authority to make national decisions, then the concept of one state, one national sovereignty, must be an essential part of the process.
It is equally clear that we cannot be a single national state if the rules are different for any one province in regard to official language. The principle of bilingualism is imposed by the British North America Act for one province alone under section 133. It is clear today that Quebec will no longer accept the status of being the only province required by the constitution to give full status to two official languages. It is the object of this bill to extend full status to the two official languages throughout Canada.
Those of us who believe in the principles of the bill are under no illusions concerning the difficulties in its practical application. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), who spoke yesterday, undertook a process of consultation
Official Languages
with the authorities in each province to determine what difficulties could be anticipated. As a result of these discussions, a series of amendments was introduced yesterday afternoon.
The amendments are designed, among other things, to reassure the spokesman for some of the western provinces who were concerned. Perhaps the most frequently expressed fear has been the possible exclusion of candidates from western Canada from the public service. The Minister of Justice yesterday cited statistics on applications from graduates of western Canadian universities indicating that these have risen very sharply. Certainly the interest in seeking employment in the public service shown by graduates of western Canadian universities has not in any way diminished but has increased.
It may be that this represents a trend which will be accentuated in future years. It may be that the students who are seeking employment in the public service are those who have had more interest in language training and who now find that the public service offers exciting career possibilities for which their language training gives them an additional qualification. But for the overwhelming majority of positions in the public service language training is not enough. The fundamental requirement must continue to be, as it always has been, competence in one's profession or work.
It is the public service aspects of the bill that give me the most concern, in part because the constituency I represent has a very large number of public servants residing within its boundaries. I note that the amendment to clause 40 proposed yesterday has the effect of re-emphasizing the basic principle of merit in regard to the duties of the Public Service Commission. There should be no hesitation whatsoever about repeating this on every occasion when any doubt is cast on its application.
In 1964 the right hon. L. B. Pearson, then Prime Minister of Canada, made a statement indicating the general principles which would guide the application of a policy of bilingualism in the public service. Mr. Pearson stated that bilingualism was to be encouraged as a matter of policy but that individuals who were recruited prior to the introduction of the bilingualism policy would not suffer any impairment of their public service careers because of their lack of knowledge of a second official language. In practice, the application of these two principles creates serious difficulties. To a considerable extent

May 21, 1969
Official Languages
they are not reconcilable. To the extent to which a bonus is given tor a second language in a promotional competition, there must be some impairment of the career ot the candidate without the second language.
It is to the credit of the Public Service Commission that they have used a great deal of sense in applying the policy directives. In my opinion there is an area of possible conflict between the legislation now before the house and the legislation which established the Public Service Commission. The Public Service Commission in effect must be the agency responsible for applying the policy of bilingualism in large sectors of the public service. Its regulations must be consistent not only with the act directly establishing it but with the intent of the official languages bill.
It is my sincere hope that the Public Service Commission will give early consideration to measures designed to give protection to the career civil servant who was recruited some time ago but is now at the stage in his life when it is most difficult to begin to learn a second language. I believe there are some special instances where an enlightened and humane policy by the Public Service Commission to protect such long service employees would be in the national interest. The Public Service Commission must also establish at the earliest possible date objective tests of language competence, not only for initial appointments but especially in promotional competitions.
In speaking to this bill last Friday the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) pointed out that there is no provision in the bill dealing with the National Capital Commission or any policy for development of the national capital. In these areas we await the final recommendations of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism and we will follow closely the statements by the minister responsible for policy in this area. It is to be hoped that the minister will make an authoritative statement in the near future in view of the speculative stories in the press in recent weeks, which have come from undisclosed sources. These speculations have done a great deal of harm and are endangering the good relations that exist between the cities of Ottawa and Hull.
I have no hesitation in supporting this bill and the principles that are embodied in it. I believe, as strongly as I believe in anything, that Canada must be built on the recognition of the rights of both official languages. As the Minister of Justice pointed out yesterday, this

bill has the support of an overwhelming majority of the younger generation in Canada. The bill itself is perhaps a prelude to the intense discussion which must take place on the amendment of our national constitution. I repeat that the bill is a cornerstone on which the constitution itself will be rebuilt.
The principles of the bill are the most effective answer to those who put forward the concept of two nations or separate status for any one province. I urge its adoption by all of those who, regardless of political affiliation, believe as I do that Canada must be one nation with two official languages from coast to coast.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot conclude my remarks without replying to the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin) who said yesterday in the house that it was a shame that at the United Nations, for example, only Englishspeaking people would speak on behalf of Canada.
If that were true, it would certainly be a shame, but it is incorrect. Two years ago, I was appointed as a member of the Canadian delegation to the general Assembly of the United Nations. Among the delegates was the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Pelletier) who, last Friday, spoke in this house about the bill under consideration.
That delegation consisted also of two ambassadors, Mr. Ignatieff, who knows several languages, and Mr. Paul Beaulieu, the present Canadian ambassador in Paris.
Therefore, the Canadian delegates were 40 per cent French-speaking.
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Charlevoix was referring yesterday to an incident which occurred several years ago, he should have said so, but he did not. We have made progress since. Our civil service is becoming increasingly bilingual. For the sake of national unity, we have to recognize the advance which we have made.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I hope all members of the house will support this bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Very briefly, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations with regard to the bill now before us. Some of them do not necessarily reflect the opinions of the New Democratic party but I believe it is only right that I
May 21. 1969



should say in this chamber what I believe to be true in this country of ours.
I was pleased to hear the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) express the view yesterday that this bill should be dealt with in the political arena rather than be surrounded by an aura of suspicion. I agree with him in this respect, and I congratulate him on that statement. I do not, of course, agree that every member who stands up in this house should parrot the statements made by members of the cabinet. Individual members have a responsibility to those in the areas from which they come to express their concern at this time. I do not believe this debate need be a lengthy one but I do believe that certain things ought to be placed on record.
I am sure no reasonable person in this country takes exception to section 133 of the British North America Act. Everyone here agrees that proper recognition should be given to the provisions of this section and that there should be no discrimination of any kind when carrying out the intent of that act. Nevertheless, it is my belief that at this time in the history of Canada we are moving on a particular course far more rapidly than the people can accept. In my view, and I say this sincerely, the people of Quebec have just cause for their suspicion of the English speaking population of Canada. During the past 100 years they have had just reason to express their suspicions, and in many cases there has been justification for the action they have taken since 1960. I think we should look at history before we form a definite attitude toward these events. In 1964, according to a professor of sociology of the University of Montreal, which I attended for a short while, only 51 out of 760 people in the corporate elite in Quebec were French Canadians. This leads one to conclude that French Canadians were virtually being eliminated from an area they were entitled to occupy.
Let us look at history further. I am not going back too far; I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will recognize the effect of the words to which I intend to refer briefly. The reason for much of the concern felt in the earlier part of this decade was that the bishops wrote to the industrialists asking them to pay low wages so that French Canadians would go back to the farms, which were the only road to heaven, and avoid occasions of sin in the cities; moreover, urban life was dominated by English speaking people.
Official Languages
As Members of Parliament go about the country and justify the bill before us, as most of us do to the best of our ability, we realize that certain ministers of the government are also moving about Canada laying the blame for some of the circumstances in which we find ourselves at the present time at the doors of the English speaking people. For myself, I think we ought to go back and determine what the facts really are. I was concerned on reading some of the statements which the minister who introduced this bill has made in various parts of the country. It is only right that we should look at these statements to determine whether or not some extremism has been shown by the minister concerned in his addresses to members of the French community throughout Canada.
I was disappointed to read in a speech released by the minister's department on December 7 in Winnipeg certain of the statements made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) to the group he was addressing. According to this release he stated that though the report of the B and B Commission had been in hand only a short time measures were already under way to implement the recommendations it contained. Well, Mr. Speaker, there have been many reports from royal commissions and task forces, including the Carter Commission and the Woods Commission, but none of them has met with the prompt action accorded by the government to the recommendations of the B and B Commission which, I might add, has not yet completed its final report. There is nothing wrong with a government taking prompt action on a report which contains good recommendations. But it seems that the government is more concerned today about acting on this particular report than it is about the reports of all the other royal commissions and task forces which have been set up in this country. It is high time the cabinet looked seriously at some of the other reports which have been submitted for perusal and took immediate action with regard to them.
The Secretary of State told his audience:
We have taken measures not only to make superficial changes but to alter fundamentally the situation which exists.
Any representative of the political parties here, or any individual politician, would be condemned by this house if he went across the country making statements of a type which could be considered extremist. But the very minister who introduced this bill into the House of Commons is guilty of extremism in making statements of the sort he has made.

May 21, 1969
Official Languages
I refer again to the hon. gentleman's speech at Winnipeg. He stated that thousands of civil servants had signed up for courses in the official languages. This I subscribe to. Then he went on:
Every year, dozens of families move to Quebec City or Toronto for a total immersion experience in French or English.
I bring this out because I feel that at this point in our history, even though 102 years have gone by since confederation, the people of this country cannot afford the extra tax burden placed on their shoulders in an attempt to make every individual bilingual. I agree with the leader of the Creditistes that this is not a process which can take place overnight. It has to be started within the school system. I want my children to become bilingual and they are taking French courses now in Ottawa schools. Effective French courses should have been available in our schools long ago. My point is that this process has to start at the bottom, not at the top.
A short while ago the minister addressed a meeting in Regina. The editor of the Moose Jaw Times-Herald, in commenting on this meeting in an article which appeared on April 18, expressed his point of view in words better than any which occur to me at this moment. The article is headed, "Realities Ignored", and reads:
The trouble with intellectuals also running the country is that, at times, their ideas may run counter to realities.
A case in point is presented by State Secretary Gerard Pelletier, one of three Quebec bright men persuaded to enter politics a few years back (the others are Prime Minister Trudeau and Mr. Marchand).
During a visit to Regina, Mr. Pelletier said he would like to see "a first class French school in every city in Canada ..." He said this would allow French Canadians to become as mobile as English Canadians.
The idea may have some merit but the practice is something else again.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
There are several reasons for suggesting the idea is impractical, for the present and many years to come.
One is that of costs, another is a very real shortage of teachers, a third is that there is no barrier to mobility at present.
Of costs, the additional burden of a strictly French school in "every city", as Mr. Pelletier would have it, suggests a high French-speaking population. And, of course, such a school would have to be from kindergarten to grade 12.
The teacher shortage has been, is and will continue to be one of the main reasons that, in the main, the teaching of French in our present system of education is so poor. It would seem to us that

the primary objective is to improve the teaching of languages in all schools rather than to aim at segregation of a type. Teaching of languages is beneficial to all people and should not be restricted to a minority.
On the subject of mobility, it will forever remain a fact of life in Canada that French Canadians who wish to move to English speaking sections will have to learn the English language. What is changing in Canada, and this is to the good, is that English speaking Canadians who are moving to Quebec must display equal desire to learn the French language.
Mr. Pelletier's suggestion may be intellectually stimulating but it ignores realities of life.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext: Certainly, sir.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member has been talking about extreme statements and mentioned two I had made. In one, I described a state of fact, which is the policy of the government. In the other, I said it was desirable to have a good French school in every major city of Canada. Would the hon. member make clear whether he considers either one or other of those statements extreme? I am asking him because I have not been able to understand what the word means as a result of the way it has been used over the last few days.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the minister I used the word "extreme" in the sense that the government believe they must implement bilingualism across Canada today. I will go on to point to some other statements that the minister made in Boston, and I believe in New York, as the sort of statements that are creating an atmosphere in Canada today which is bringing about an animosity between east and west that I do not like.
I have just referred to an editorial and I quoted not my own words but those of the writer of the editorial, who I might point out is a French Canadian. The part of the statement that is extreme is that the minister now says it is essential to have a French school in every major city in Canada. If the minister did not say that, then I should like him to clear up the matter now. If he did, then I think my point is well taken when I say that municipal taxation across Canada today is such that we simply cannot afford this type of luxury. I would be the first to agree entirely with the principle behind the language bill, but I would be the last to agree that the people of this nation today can afford the luxury of a French school in every community, as the minister says as he goes across the country addressing various groups.
May 21. 1969

I sincerely suggest to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that he tread very softly, carefully and slowly in the over-all implementation of bilingualism across Canada. I know of too many senior citizens at the present time who are losing their homes as a result of taxation. As a former alderman of the city of Moose Jaw I know that 53 cents out of every dollar goes toward education, and this cost is increasing all the time. If the minister will stand in his place and say that the federal government will absorb the added cost of implementing bilingualism in every major city of Canada, then I personally will applaud him forever and a day. But I know this will not be the case.
The cost of education in this country is on the upswing and will continue to be so. Unless the federal government absorbs more responsibility for the cost of education, this whole country will collapse because of the dilemma facing our seniors whom we revere so much but who cannot pay their way. I am sure every member of the house realizes there are too many other things in this country requiring immediate action besides bilingualism.
I am not saying for one moment that bilingualism itself is not important, because I believe it is. It is very important for the mobility of people across the country. I am sure the editor of the Moose Jaw Times-Herald. recognizes that fact. As he puts it, he recognizes the facts of life.
A former minister in the present Liberal government has stated that the intellectuals are forgetting the nuts and bolts of the situation. I subscribe to that statement. Intellectuals cannot run this country because they do not provide the bread and butter to those who need it.
This point has already been made so I will not belabour it. I realize the minister has given some explanation as far as employees of the National Capital Commission and the museums are concerned, but I want to make the point that anybody who is hired in the civil service or in a government agency should be bilingual if that is one of the conditions of his employment. But I do not buy a situation where conditions of employment are changed after people have been hired and have been employed for a good many years.
Throughout my working days-I do not know whether I am still working but that is beside the point-I have belonged to a trade union, and I have always objected to a company changing conditions of employment
Official Languages
after an agreement has been signed. I earnestly plead with the minister not to change the conditions of employment of those already employed in the civil service. Do not change the conditions or place of employment of guards at museums and other public buildings.
I think it is a national disgrace when a man who has served as a guard or commissionaire at the front door of a public building is relegated to the back door or some other place. It is a national disgrace when this government or any other government deliberately takes a man from where he has been rightfully employed for many years and relegates him to some other position. I think the minister should give due consideration to this question. Some of these men are in their later years, and until they retire I suggest that other personnel be made available to serve those who speak only French.
Too many things have been said throughout this nation which are regrettable from the minister's point of view, as well as from my point of view as a Canadian. But let me assure the minister that if his desire to unite all of Canada is sincere he will have the co-operation of every person in Canada. I can also assure the minister that if he is insincere and uses unfairly the provision in the bill whereby the Governor in Council may make such regulations as he deems necessary to effect compliance with the act and the conduct of affairs by the government of Canada and its departments and agencies, then Canada will no longer exist as a country.
One other statement of the minister of which he should be aware and to which I personally have taken great offence was made when he addressed a certain group of people in Boston. I do not have the date of his speech but I am sure he will recognize it. At page 7 of his address he said:
From 1867 to 1960, our country, like yours, underwent a period of immense economic development. But compared to yours-
He is talking about the United States.
-our political and cultural life seems dull and somewhat monotonous.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I do not subscribe to statements of this sort made by Canadians going to other countries. In my own province the premier is continually making statements outside the province which condemn and damn the very province of which he is a native. I do not endorse the actions of people who deliberately declare in other places that life in Canada seems dull

May 21, 1969
Official Languages
and somewhat monotonous. I do not think the past 100 years in Canada have been dull and monotonous. I can assure the minister that even with the implementation of the language bill we will continue to fulfil our moral obligations. I do not think the people in the province of Quebec and elsewhere appreciate the minister condemning in this and other countries what we have known in the past to be a fact of life. We are Canadians, and the minister should realize this fact when making speeches outside this country. I am certain the people of the province of Quebec realize this without the language bill, although I am sure it will bind us more closely together.
I plead with the minister not to move too quickly on the language bill. When travelling throughout the country addressing public meetings we can explain the situation as it should be explained. If inflammatory statements such as I have referred to continue to be made, the language bill will not be regarded in the context the minister and every member of this house wishes, I ask the minister and the cabinet to go slowly with the regulations and give the people time to be educated in the two languages. Let the two languages work into the employment of this country. Do not insist that civil servants at all levels become bilingual immediately.
I am sure most people in my constituency do not oppose the language bill. They are just as proud as I to be Canadians. They are very concerned about the cost of implementing the language bill. They are also concerned about provisions such as clause 10 which may mean that every railway employee in this country, every civil servant and every employee of a crown corporation could be required to learn to speak both languages at a very late time in their lives. It would not be easy for me at the age of 42 to learn a second language. However, I will be willing to make an attempt when I have the opportunity next year. To ask the people of this country to learn a second language would burden them with additional municipal debt. The economics of this country today will not permit it unless the government will assume the complete cost of the entire implementation of the language bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
As this is my first effort, Mr. Speaker,, let me at the outset make the solemn pledge to Your Honour and hon. members that I will not at any time needlessly take up the time of the house simply to speak as often as some other hon.

members, or for the benefit of indirectly influencing a few voters, or to further my personal position or gain. I will speak only when I have something of substance and significance to say for my constituents or for the good of our country. I sincerely hope Your Honour will call me to order whenever my words do not reflect this substance or significance.
The bill now under discussion is of paramount importance to Canada and to my constituency. Of my constituents, 45 per cent are bilingual citizens of French extraction. I deem it most important that the small number of French speaking members in this house who are not from the province of Quebec should bring the viewpoint of their French Canadian constituents forcefully and clearly to the attention of the house. French speaking members from the province of Quebec cannot possibly represent our thinking and attitude any more than can the English speaking members. I therefore hope every French Canadian member from other than the province of Quebec, without regard to party, will speak in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, during the electoral, campaign, I said to the French Canadians in the constituency of Timmins that this is now our last chance to remain French Canadians in Canada, outside Quebec, and that, besides, our fate rests mainly with the Quebecers.
My opponents took exception to that statement, but my constituents elected me so that I could come here and say it again. For us, French Canadians from outside Quebec, it is our last chance to remain French Canadians, and it is the Quebecers who will finally decide.
This is quite clear. How can we justify our language in Canada, if Quebec is not a part of Canada? Without Quebec, it would disappear immediately and completely. And why not? Why should the other Canadian citizens be interested in French Canadians if the French Canadians in Quebec felt no concern at all about those people who number one and a quarter million?
The separatists claim they want to preserve language and culture. Nevertheless, through a simple decision, namely to separate, they would jeopardize the future of a million and a quarter French Canadians. That is how the separatists would safeguard things.
More than a million and a quarter French Canadians would be abandoned and they want us to believe that it would be to protect
May 21, 1969

us. What nonsense, what kind of argument is that? And that without ever consulting any of the one and a quarter million people interested. What a civilized way of doing it.
Mr. Rene Levesque said in Timmins and I heard him with my own ears:
Let the French Canadian people in Ontario look after themselves. What do you want us to do? We must look after ourselves, in Quebec.
That is intelligent.
Mr. Levesque also said: French Canadians outside Quebec asked me to work out a policy aimed at bringing them back to Quebec; it is the only way for them to remain French Canadians. I do not know where his information comes from, but he is completely off the track. He should contact other people than separatists if he wants to get accurate facts.
My father was born in Saint-Anaclet, near Rimouski, and my mother was from Cap-Saint-Ignace, near Montmagny. Can you beat that for being a Quebecer? And I can tell Mr. Levesque straight out that never would my father agree to go back to Quebec under any circumstances. I can tell him that it would never be to my interest to move to Quebec.
He would never be able to convince even 100 French Canadians, out of 30,000 or more in our constituency, to move to Quebec-not that we do not like Quebec, because, on the contrary, Quebecers and ourselves are all the same-but just because our homeplace is the Timmins riding. Why would they move? They left Quebec because they had reasons to do so. Since they did not go back, they also had reasons not to. Why would these people give up good salaries for smaller ones, interesting jobs for less attractive ones, the advantages of bilingualism for narrow unilin-gualism? Mr. Levesque is just day-dreaming and altering facts.
In my constituency, I know a young girl who was a strong supporter of the separatist movement and who last summer was the lucky winner of a trip to France. She now deplores the separatists' fate and never stops criticizing France where social life, according to her, is fifty years behind ours in Canada.
Mr. Levesque is also saying that we are dead ducks and that we will not survive. What a mistake! What a misguided notion! What blindness!
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The same thing applies to those who advocate unilingualism in Quebec. We are told that it is to preserve the French language; but how can it be done by passing a law,
Official Languages
without consulting anyone? That would deny the right of 1,250,000 French Canadians who live outside Quebec to the French language! That is exactly what would happen, because, how could we justify the teaching of French in Ontario schools, if Quebec should refuse the teaching of English in its schools? You see, that does not make any sense.
At the beginning of the session, Mr. Speaker, I heard the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin) say that he was speaking as a French Canadian from Quebec and on behalf of the other French Canadians from the remainder of the country. I should ask the hon. member to give us his support, his attention, his interest, but I would ask him, for heaven's sake, not to speak on our behalf. Too often, some people who do not know what we think at all, claim they are our spokesmen without ever consulting us. They have their own interests and do not understand our way of thinking. That is why I say to the hon. member: "Support us, but for heaven's sake, do not speak in our name."
Mr. Speaker, last fall, I heard the hon. member for Temiscamingue say what is reported in Hansard at page 1494. I wish to congratulate him sincerely. I have a great deal of admiration for him. I sincerely believe that he has done at least as much as anybody else to promote bilingualism at the federal level. The hon. member was telling us that three of his colleagues, who did not speak English, had been arrested by an Ottawa policeman who did not speak French. As my hon. friend, I think that the policeman in question would be able to perform his duties more efficiently if he could speak French.
But, on the other hand, how can the members who do not speak Ehglish serve their electors adequately since they cannot even talk with the English-speaking members or get to know what they think?
True, we are provided with simultaneous interpretation in the House of Commons, but parliament does not consist of the House of Commons only. Communications must be established with people outside the house. Therefore, I earnestly suggest to the hon. members to register immediately for an English course. What applies to Englishspeaking Canadians also holds good for French-speaking Canadians. Such action on their part will prove their sincerity.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to tell our brothers from the province of Quebec who, for the .major part, have not yet agreed to separatism, to whom we feel very close and of

May 21, 1969
Official Languages
whom we are proud, not to be taken in by slogans, misleading catch phrases, shallow statements and policies that offer crumbs to everyone, not bread.
I also tell them: Look carefully into those policies and, I entreat you, speak your mind. Do not let the remainder of Canada think that those separatists represent the public opinion in Quebec, and that they are a majority. Do not become yourselves separatists by not taking a stand. Denounce those hypocritical and evil-minded trouble makers. Do you believe that those mean trouble makers, that the great general who has now left the political stage, that a frustrated Minister of Cultural Affairs, that a very narrow-minded school board, are going to preserve and develop the French language in the province of Quebec and in the rest of Canada? Not at all! That will rather depend on the initiative of every French Canadian everywhere on the sound judgment of the great majority of politicians in Canada on the good-will of the great majority of citizens everywhere and, above all, on the influence of Quebec within Canada.
I entreat the province of Quebec not to forsake the million and a quarter French Canadians who are not living in Quebec. Our ancestors left their homes and their families to go out and spread the French fact throughout Canada. Are we going to let their efforts go to waste?
Those good people have spread all over Canada and have multiplied to the point that they now number one and a quarter million. All this was to develop and reinforce the French fact in Canada. Are we going to allow the results of their struggle to amount to nothing? It would likely have been much easier for our people to stay home. But if they had not had the courage to spread, if they had refused to leave, if they had not foreseen our vast bilingual country, where would we be now? The French language and culture would no longer exist outside Quebec. We would not have Canada as we know it today. Let us not thank them by forgetting them. Let us not show our appreciation by denying them. Let us continue to give them our support and our encouragement.

The final test, Mr. Speaker, is here and now. As at the end of a school year students eventually have to face examinations, so this parliament must now face the test of two official languages. The statements, the promises, the positions have looked good. They have reassured to a large degree, but now is

the time when the law must guarantee. There is no turning back. And, Mr. Speaker, now that the principle has been established, now that the formula has been enunciated, I am completely amazed at the weak excuses that are appearing to delay further, to suspend, to sidetrack, and to evade the decision.
What a laugh when I hear some say, "We agree with the law but we should have it tested constitutionally!" What hypocrisy, what baloney when they say, "Sure, we should have two official languages, but it is too costly!" What of the cost to parents of private French schools which are just now beginning to receive reasonable government support? And what about the economic and social costs of the drop-outs from the French schools because of the too great financial burden on the parents, who pay twice for their children's education?
What rubbish when they say two official languages will mean discrimination in the civil service! What about the arrogant discrimination that went on for years and years, even in the heart of Quebec, and in national transport agencies? Where has the fair play been in all those instances? Where is it today? Are we ready to accept our responsibilities? Have we matured enough? Have we the courage to call a spade a spade and stand and be counted, yes or no, clearly and honestly?
My French ancestors came to Canada in 1623. That is a long time ago. Does this mean that I am more Canadian than he who came here in 1923? Of course not. Does the fact that my ancestors were French while someone else's were English make me more Canadian than him? Of course not. Does the fact that I speak two languages while someone else speaks only one make me more Canadian? Of course not.
But, Mr. Speaker, let no man-I say no man-tell me that I do not fit in in Canada because I am French Canadian. Let no man tell me that I will have to speak English because he does not speak French. Many people do not want to be hyphenated Canadians. Why not? What is wrong with being a hyphenated Canadian? Canada would not be Canada if it did not have hyphenated Canadians. We would all be Americans. Canada is Canada and Canadians are Canadians because we have two great working languages, because we have many nationalities and many cultures, all this tempered by the influence of the huge American society to the south of us. What is wrong with that? These
May 21, 1969

are the reasons it is great to be Canadian and it is great to remain Canadian.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said in the house last December, as recorded on page 3929 of Hansard, that the French Canadians had been given bilingual cheques. In a Prime Minister's career, what a pitiful contribution to look back to! What sadness must be in his heart today-

There are as many French Canadians outside Quebec as there are people in Alberta. They will be there speaking French after the hon. member is gone, after his children are gone and after his grandchildren are gone. Let us not search the past for legal loopholes, for traditional balderdash, for old
Official Languages
prejudices, for feelings of bigotry, for any excuse to oppose the two languages.
I was pleased the other day by a choice bit of wisdom on the part of one of my constituents. The gentleman in question spent considerable time decrying the official languages bill to me. He expressed his completely partial viewpoint that French has no place in Canada outside Quebec. He made a very strong representation against the bill. Then he said-
