speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy for me to rise to speak on this bill. I realize that whichever side one takes on a subject such as this one will find oneself being accused of prejudice. This bill, on the face of it at least, would seem to be acceptable, but when one delves a little deeper and explores the possible application of the bill one must, I think, have reservations which I should like to put forward at this

May 21, 1969
Official Languages
time. I shall not go into the constitutional aspect of the bill. Other members have covered this principle. I shall not struggle with the bill in terms of its legal aspects. This, of course, is a field which is foreign to me. I shall deal with the bill in terms of how I consider it relates to human beings, national unity and the community in which I live.
First, from the point of view of nations becoming great and from the point of view of national unity I think history will bear me out in my observation that the melting pot theory is far more successful than the mosaic theory and that nations have become great not by emphasizing the differences in people but by projecting their similarities. If this were legislation that would do away with all records of racial origin and all the requirements for records of racial origin, I could give it my unequivocal support, then we could get down to the business of being Canadians instead of having this endless haggle over English and French.
Many of my closest friends are of French origin. Many of them are of other nationalities. I come from a part of the country where men and women are taken at face value, for what they are, not who they are, and where race, colour, creed and, I might add, racial origin mean nothing. So it is rather mystifying and strange to me to come to this portion of Canada where a person's ancestry means so much. It is not evident to me that your idealistic theories on the beautiful mosaic of culture and creed have brought you very much unity or as much genuine understanding in the 300 years you have been here in eastern Canada as I think we have achieved in 80 years with our melting pot theory in the west.
If there is one mistake that we made in this country which we should remember it is the mistake we made in respect of our Indian population. One hundred years ago we made them different in a way far in excess of merely their colour or creed. We set them apart on islands unto themselves and called these islands reservations. We did not stop there. We looked after them by giving them special privileges and concessions as well. There is no need for me to finish that story. But is there not a parallel that can be drawn with the situation which confronts us here? I say, let requirements of culture and language fall as they may by the law of supply and demand, or should I say in the light of a language situation by supply and demand. I have travelled this country from coast to

coast. I have heard much of the English majority and the French minority. Statements of this kind, however, do not bear close scrutiny.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
With relation now to western Canada and taking this figure from current statistics, I notice that 50 per cent of the people in the prairie provinces list their racial origins as other than English or French. Therefore, if we are going to be totally accurate we have to say that the population is comprised of Canadians of all ethnic origins including German, Ukrainian, Polish, Italian, Chinese, English, Scandinavians and a dozen others, the majority of whom use the English language in business. If we consider the number of minority groups in Canada, certainly we must conclude that those Canadians of French descent constitute one of the two majorities. With this mixture of people thrown together in this country, the farther we stay away from guarantees and special concessions to any group, the closer we will come to achieving what surely must be our ultimate goal-a united and strong Canada and a better standard of living.
For a moment I should like to dwell on what one might term a Trojan horse quality in respect of this proposed legislation. It may be that the government has no other intent in respect of this bill than that already expressed openly by its sponsors and authors. The fact remains that the terms of the bill make it capable of manipulation by determined and unscrupulous people toward the achievement of ends which would be impossible to attain directly and openly.
The organization and procedures envisaged in this bill are such as to open the door to the worst kind of political philandering and manipulation. As I read the terms of the bill it is open to any small group or even a single person, wholeheartedly dedicated to advancing the cause of the French language and culture across Canada, to arrange things so that a 10 per cent area could be created within any province. Because of the structure and terms of the bill, and because of the machinery provided to protect and nurture such areas, there is little doubt that such an area once established would flourish and grow despite the disproportionate cost which would be required in government effort and expenditure.
We must now consider such an area, duly established under this legislation, in the light
May 21, 1969

of what other benefits it might receive from existing federal legislation and legislation yet to come. I have in mind all the resources available to bolster and assist such areas, including those now available under this government, particularly from departments like that of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier). On the purely economic side I think of the vast resources already at the arbitrary beck and call of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). In view of the public speeches and statements of the two gentlemen at present holding these two portfolios, it would not be unreasonable to expect that they might pay more attention and give more assistance to one of these newly set-up areas. Of course the statements of the Prime Minister did nothing to allay the fears in this regard. Let me read from his statement to the constitutional conference held in Ottawa. He said:
I repeat today, in the name of the federal government, that we are prepared to consider the provision by the federal government to the provinces who want to deal with the minorities in their province of the other official language, providing to them technical or financial assistance of one kind or another.
I will not labour that because I think it speaks for itself.
Let me go on to say that this bill contains the seeds of a plant about which we know nothing. We do not know, nor have we any way of calculating, what shape it will assume as it grows, what it will look like or what its characteristics may be. We are assured by the sponsors of this legislation, including the Prime Minister, that it will have an innocent and beneficial bloom. Watered by the cultural theories of the Secretary of State and generously fertilized by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, it could grow into a monster and choke off the healthy growth of our nation, causing untold problems.
I suppose one might say that the ultimate extension of possibilities inherent in this bill might lead into the political field. Once a 10 per cent area was established as a special bilingual area it could be carefully nursed through federal government assistance to the point of development where it would invite gerrymandering in the future redistribution of federal electoral seats. We should remember that such areas, once established, will inevitably attract special attention and treatment from Ottawa. This could only be done at the expense of equality in the treatment afforded other provincial centres. None of
Official Languages
these things may happen, but in all seriousness I suggest that the possibility they will is in essence the basis of this legislation. There can be little doubt that its provisions make this entirely possible.
I should like to point out at this time that some of the objections voiced against this bill, objections which I notice are coming at least in part from western Canada, are based on economic grounds and have to some extent been built up by discontent with the province of Quebec. Many of these involve small matters, probably oversights on the part of busy cabinet ministers. One might say they are not related to this bill at all, but in context with the position of the west they are relatively important. Let me cite a few examples.
I quote from a submission presented by the Manitoba Dairy Commission which states in part that there has been a transfer of the dairy products quota from the prairie provinces, amounting to 8,300,000 pounds, to the province of Quebec. This means in round figures a reduction to Manitoba of two million pounds, four million pounds to Saskatchewan, and two million pounds to Alberta. This does not in itself seem too bad, but when the people out west realize that they import 14 million pounds of butter from the province of Quebec, in respect of which the Canadian Dairy Commission is paying the shipping costs to the prairies, one can understand their discontent.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I quote from a report of the Western Hog Growers Association which is contained in the Edmonton Journal of April 11. This article states that the federal feed freight assistance and storage policy is a direct subsidy to eastern hog growers. It is calculated that this program subsidized Quebec hog growers to the extent of $8.10 per animal last year, compared with a subsidy of 40 cents in the western provinces.
I have another example, Mr. Speaker. I was thumbing through the order paper and noticed that 132 post offices were built in the province of Quebec in 1968, whereas in a province with a greater population, Ontario, only 72 were built or a little more than half the number built in Quebec. In Alberta only 13 post offices were built in that year, and poor old Manitoba had to settle for nine.
All these things contribute to the opposition to this bill. There is nothing wrong with our basic program of building post offices. There is nothing wrong with much of our present

May 21, 1969
Official Languages
dairy policy. There is perhaps nothing wrong with the laudable aims presented on the face of this languages bill. But the crux of the matter is the interpretation and administration of these policies and laws. This is where the bind will come. Do we have confidence in the men who have established these policies and will administer the law? If we do not, are we not just opening up new avenues to advance inequality under the guise of equality?
I object to this legislation on other grounds, Mr. Speaker. To my mind it represents an attempt to do good by the wrong means. I do not believe the cause of bilingualism or national unity will be well served by resorting to law and compulsion. The legalistic approach reflected in the government's attempt to ram this legislation through parliament can lead only to endless trouble, needless expense and the creation of yet another bureaucratic monster, an expensive monster, to say the least. It will breed opposition to French language rights where none is now present. It will harden attitudes hopelessly in some areas of this country. There still exists a very good chance that opposition across Canada to the general acceptance of the French language can be overcome by time, experience and a policy of voluntary gradualism. In my opinion nothing will more quickly bring about the doom of this policy than any suggestion of compulsion or coercion.
There are in this country very few areas in which all these services are not now provided. This legislation could very well defeat its purpose and spawn resentment. If we impose bilingualism, not on the basis of its own intrinsic virtues but on arbitrary and highly questionable grounds, we will only widen the breach between French Canada and the rest of the country. No one can argue that Canadians being able to speak two languages is not a good thing. I have a very earnest desire to be bilingual. This is an achievement that brings great benefit to anyone. But the way to achieve general proficiency in both languages and general acceptance of the use of two languages must rest upon individual desire and co-operation, not on compulsion of federal law and enforced acceptance thereof.
It would be well if supporters of legislation such as this reconsidered the matter and studied closely the dual language problems of countries such as Switzerland, Belgium and South Africa. Let them study the background and evolution of language use in these nations and then compare the language conditions

that exist in those countries. Perhaps even more important, the supporters of this legislation should take into consideration the attitude of the province of Quebec in this matter. This legislation has been received by the authorities of that province in a manner which, if one were entirely charitable, would be called something less than enthusiastic.
In addition, the general trend expressed by the leading men of all political parties in Quebec has been toward a unilingual, not bilingual, province. If the heart and home of French Canada, the cultural and linguistic core of the French Canadian society, is not in favour of this legislation or even of the concept of national bilingualism, how can we expect residents of Alberta, British Columbia or Newfoundland to be enthusiastic?
I shall not dwell upon the objections as to the cost the passage of this bill will entail. It is obvious that duplication of services and facilities will require a vastly increased amount of money which can only be raised by taxation. There remains the unknown and incalculable heritage that this bill will impose upon Canadians of generations to come. I foresee this heritage as only a fertile producer of trouble and more problems. At best, this legislation will create an unseen, unspoken barrier for the stubbornly unilingual, no matter of what racial origin. This shadow barrier will be erected and bolstered by federal legislation. Even now this barrier exists in some areas.
In the public service of Canada bilingualism is the dominant, though hidden, fact of life. In the public service of today it is an unmentioned but potent condition of employment, and certainly of advancement. If this policy is further buttressed by legislation such as that now before us, it will effectively debar from the public service all but a handful of Canadians whose mother tongue is other than French. If such an obvious step is taken to alienate western Canadian citizens from their capital and central government, it will not be surprising if the voice of western separatism becomes louder and louder.
This bill has been advanced on the premise that it will reinforce national unity. But in my estimation, Mr. Speaker, the passage of the bill could very well serve, no matter how well intentioned it is, only to disunite the people of Canada in the years to come.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the notable features of this debate has been the general support by spokesmen of all parties in the house for the
May 21, 1969



principle of this bill. There has been a responsible approach to the issue of the official languages bill; hon. members have spoken responsibly and well in support of the measure. As a member of the government ranks, I have listened with great and appreciative interest to the remarks of certain opposition members.
Politics makes strange bedfellows. We have just heard a speech, not a notable one, delivered by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey). If all the actions which we contemplate in this house were to be judged only in terms of the worst eventualities of those actions, nothing would ever be accomplished by the House of Commons. Indeed, if the same philosophy had been applied to the field of invention the motor car would never have been invented because it is a danger to the pedestrian by virtue of the fact that cars travel upon roads. It was not the kind of speech which is a vote of confidence in Canada.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I happen to have on my desk a speech made by Rene Levesque as reported in the Toronto Star of April 28, 1969. He said the same thing as did the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey). Addressing himself to a cheering audience in Montreal he said: "We are taking Quebec out in five years. There will be no confederation any longer". He said that the government of Canada "denies English Canada this efficient centralization which it needs while at the same time tries to impose by force a fundamental amendment on biculturalism which it never wanted."
The hon. member for Battle River must have been reading Mr. Levesque's speech. But Mr. Levesque and separatists in all parts of Canada have a vested interest in making sure that nothing is ever done on the issue of culture and language. They are the only ones who will profit immeasurably from the continuation of the historical misunderstanding which has plagued Canada from coast to coast. It does not matter what language a separatist speaks-and they are not all confined to one province in Canada-he does not want any kind of rapprochement at all in this country because he knows the jig is up if there is any kind of agreement or better understanding between the two linguistic groups which founded this country. The hon. member for Battle River can have Mr. Rene Levesque. He may agree with his philosophy and he can get additional speeches made by him and quote from them, but the majority of
Official Languages
the members of this house will not support him.
I am not saying that it is our party's exclusive concern to ensure the future of this country and to protect the rights of our citizens. Any member in any party in this house who makes that claim is being dishonest because it is not true. I have many friends in the house who are in other parties than I am and they have made very good speeches on this subject. I may disagree with them but they have as great a concern in keeping this country strong and united as I have, and I gladly admit it. I do not care about what might have been said from political platforms.
A few hon. members have spoken in opposition to the principle of the bill. I hope that despite this apparent disagreement, members of this house are going to provide unanimous support in the vote on second reading involving the principle of the bill. It does not matter whether there is disagreement now because we have to remember that we are going to refer the bill to a special committee which should call before it as many witnesses as possible to provide the assurance to members in all parts of the house that no one's rights will be violated in this country. We should hear from people concerned about civil servants and people concerned about the cost which the implementation of this bill will entail. That point was well made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg). There is a legitimate concern in some parts of this country about the cost. This is certainly so in British Columbia although, as hon. members know, it will not cost very much in that province. Nevertheless there is concern about the cost in British Columbia as well as in other provinces.
Some hon. members have spoken as if approval of the principle of the bill will somehow destroy for all time the possibility of change or amendment. In fact, if we expedite second reading of this measure we will have the bill in committee where it should be right now so that members of all parties can subject it to scrutiny, and some of them are pretty talented in that field. If, after reviewing the testimony of witnesses and examining evidence, these members remain intransigent in their opposition, they will have every opportunity to register that opposition when the bill comes back to the house. They will have the right to vote against it if they wish to do so at that time. However, it would be a fine thing at least to have the unanimous consent of all hon. members to send the bill to the committee in the first place.

May 21, 1969
Official Languages
A word must be said about those on the opposition side of the house who have shown restraint during the discussion of the language bill. The language bill is a very tempting target for political demagogues and there are a few of them across the country, though I am not suggesting in this house. During this debate I think the chamber has been remarkably free of political demagoguery. Perhaps no other measure touching on our emotions to such a great extent, which has come before parliament,, has provided such an opportunity for the construction of ramshackle arguments fabricated to stir public emotions and even hatred. Creating straw men and then knocking them down is an old political practice and the grand national sport of some people in public life. To an admirable extent most hon. members have taken the high road and have rejected the temptation to advance thinly disguised prejudices.
Efforts have been made to relate this measure to Rosenberg's racial theories in Nazi Germany, to suggest that this bill will make Canada into a banana republic and that the bill represents compulsion. 1 believe that a sinister kind of compulsion is suggested. These are arguments without credibility. Some hon. members have professed to see in the bill a violation of the B.N.A. Act. This is a legitimate concern on the part of some people. Of course, the same document is cited on occasion by these very same speakers as being outmoded and out of tune with the times. We heard an excellent speech by the Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) as recorded at page 54 of Hansard of September 16, 1968. At that time he said:
I am sure Canadians hope that when we are ready with reforms and amendments to our constitution we shall be able to achieve those reforms and those amendments here in Canada.
He was speaking for the official opposition and urging constitutional reform. Yet some spokesmen in this debate have stood in their places and said that this bill is a violation of that sacred precept, the B.N.A. Act. They say that the bill is out of tune with the times and that the B.N.A. Act is a sacred precept which must not be questioned. Let us remember that if we are prepared to challenge this measure on the grounds of constitutional violation we will open to question a number of actions in many fields, including every other piece of legislation dealing with the French or English language adopted by the federal authorities since the year 1867. It would not be a very profitable discussion, but perhaps it would be a field day for the lawyers.

There is a general consensus in all the parties today that there is nothing sacrosanct about the B.N.A. Act. It stood the test of time and some of it is relevant today but some of its provisions have become irrelevant, obsolete and detrimental to the development of Canada. All the parties recognize this. Our party does not have a monopoly on this view.
Some hon. members have said in this debate that economic problems are more important than linguistic or cultural matters. The point has been made time and time again that we cannot leave aside the resolution of Canada's basic problems other than culture and language, and of course that is entirely correct. However, it is a misinterpretation of the views of the government to suggest that this is the intent of the government. On October 17 of last year the Prime Minister said the following, and I quote from page 1487 of Hansard of that day:
-it is a dangerous illusion to think that this resolution and the bill which will follow are the most important aspects of the problem of Canadian unity, important though they are. Even more important is the problem of poverty and of economic and social inequality across this country. It is the continuation of inequality and poverty that creates a real threat to our future. It is a well established sociological fact that nothing so much as economic and social insecurity produces deep prejudice which expresses itself in language and in social and racial disorder.
Of course we have to move on these other fronts as well. We have to move on the problems of poverty, regional inequality, housing, and all the others.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Why don't we do so now?
Another hon. Member: We will, next year.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
No, this year. In other words, the government recognizes that the language bill by itself will not bring about the abolition of inequality. It is but one goal along the road to a better Canada.
The question is asked: Who stands to gain from the passage of the official languages bill? I suggest that the vast majority of Canadians in all provinces who want a strong and united country will gain from this bill. Who stands to lose the most? As I said earlier, separatists do, whatever their language, whatever their region. Separatism thrives on hate, discord and misunderstanding. Separatists want to drive a wedge between one part of Canada and the other. Separatists, whatever their language, counsel despair. We have an example in Rene Levesque. They counsel despair. It does not matter where they live. This is their language.
May 21, 1969

[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Here are some quotations I have gathered from various sources: "We'd be better off by ourselves. Let's have a unilingual state.. . Economically we would thrive." And: "We would be far more prosperous if we did not have to subsidize the rest of Canada." Where have we heard that before? A small handful [DOT]of equally embittered men in other areas say: "The game's over. We are totally unconcerned about whether or not French language rights are extended in other parts of Canada. We shall go our own separate way." The siren song sung to the people of Toronto is: "You people in English speaking Canada need not worry at all about granting rights to people of French origin in other parts of the country because they will not last, in any case."
What is the true nature of the game these forces are playing? It is to alienate one province from another, to drive the country apart for the sake of their own egotistical political ambitions, to leave unattended the rancours and misunderstandings of history to the end that they may eventually destroy the Canada we know, a Canada cherished by all members of his house regardless of party.
So we have this bill before us. It is not a perfect bill. It is a bill which seeks to provide within certain realistic, even modest limits, guarantees for English speaking groups where French predominates and for French language groups where English predominates. It is often forgotten that it is a two-way bill, a bill which expresses the determination of almost all of us that the will of the people of Canada made clear by this parliament shall prevail over the narrow, insular, hate-wracked views of separatists wherever they may live in this nation.
No longer shall these mischief-makers be able to say: "The French minority is being persecuted in other parts of Canada; let us provide a haven here; let us become an independent state and then we can call them all home." No longer will other shrill separatist voices be able to trumpet the theme: "English language rights are being suppressed in French Canada. . Let Quebec go, and the sooner the better...We would do better on our own.", We have heard that in western Canada. We westerners know. Probably people in eastern Canada have heard it, too.
Of course the bill is not perfect. Nevertheless it represents at least a partial antidote to the hatreds which form the arsenal of separatists everywhere. As the Prime Minister has
Official Languages
said, those who argue for separation in whatever form are prisoners of past injustice, blind to the possibilities of the future. The only people who will object to this bill are those who lack a vision of Canada in 1969 and beyond.
If we say to the French speaking Canadian who wants to remain a Canadian that the only place where he can be a French speaking citizen is in Quebec, we are making him look upon Quebec, not Canada, as the sole protector of his language and culture. And Canada would be the loser. If we say to the English speaking Canadian who wants to remain a Canadian that the only place where he can be an English speaking citizen is outside Quebec, we are making him look upon Ontario, British Columbia, or one of the other provinces as the protector of his language and culture. And again Canada would be the loser.
The official languages bill provides guarantees that Canadians can look to the central government not to any one provincial government, for the preservation and development of the language and culture of their language groups, and it guarantees, as well that the rights of all people, of either ethnic origin or of all ethnic origins, will be protected.
Together with others from my province I have received letters of support for this measure as well as letters of condemnation. I have quite an interesting file on the subject, and I am sure other hon. members have one as well. Most of the letters in opposition stem, I am convinced, from a misunderstanding of the bill. The measure has been widely misinterpreted, perhaps innocently in most cases, as an attempt to force English speaking Canadians to learn French. Some suggest it is solely an attempt to make French an official language in areas where there is a French speaking population of at least 10 per cent. Yet, as one western newspaper has stated editorially, it has been overlooked that English has also become an official language in areas throughout Quebec where there is an English speaking population of at least 10 per cent.
As enunciated yesterday by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), it is the government's wish and intention to avoid a confrontation in the courts over the constitutionality of this measure. It is to be hoped-and I express this hope as one who spent some time in a provincial legislature

that the western provinces will not choose to challenge this proposed act. Among other reasons, the bill as outlined will affect the western provinces only to a minimal extent. The delay brought about by a

May 21, 1969
Official Languages
challenge in the Supreme Court would result in unfairness to minority language citizens in provinces in which the act would be widely applicable.
It should be of interest to those who read into this bill a desire of the government to impose compulsory bilingualism that if we apply the bilingual district recommendations contained in the B and B report, British Columbia would have not one single bilingual district. Alberta would have one, Saskatchewan one-I suggest that Battle River voters should please note-and Manitoba, four. The provinces of New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec, each of which has expressed an interest in bilingual services, would have no fewer than 43 bilingual districts among them. New Brunswick would have eight. Ontario would have 11. Quebec, where the minority language to be protected and served under the proposed act would be English, would have 24 English language bilingual districts. So there would be 24 in Quebec and two in Saskatchewan, the home of Battle River.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext: No, no. Alberta.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext: Is it Alberta? I am sorry.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext: Get your facts right.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. I apologize to the people of Saskatchewan.
As was pointed out so well in one of the leading western newspapers, the Edmonton Journal, on February 4, 1969:
If a constitutional challenge is launched, four provinces, involved to the extent of six bilingual districts, would be delaying for years the implementation of federal bilingual services in three provinces involved to the extent of 43 bilingual districts.
In effect, it would deny English speaking residents in Quebec in 24 of these proposed districts the rights to which they are entitled. For reasons which the Minister of Justice gave yesterday there seems to be no valid ground now, if any existed at any time, for a challenge in the Supreme Court. The history of this proposed legislation is one of discussion, consultation and efforts to avoid confrontation. At the federal-provincial conference in February suggestions were made that Ottawa should consult with the provinces when contemplating programs which directly affect the provincial interest. In my opinion there is at least partial validity to the arguments put forward by the provincial premiers in this connection. In the case of the official languages bill, this

process of consultation began last October. There has not been a measure in the history of the Canadian parliament concerning which there has been more useful consultation. It has been a two-way dialogue between the provinces and the federal government.
Changes have been proposed in the area of the direct implementation of the bill. I, for one, welcome enthusiastically the amendment which reaffirms and restates the policy of maximum attention to merit in matters concerning hiring and promotion in the civil service, crown corporations and the armed forces. It cannot be emphasized too strongly that hiring policy as it affects civil servants and advancement in the public service must start first of all on the basis of ability to do the job. Willingness, or the ability, to speak the other language must be regarded as a merit factor but competence to perform the assignment must be the top priority with no discrimination shown on any other ground.
It is a constructive proposal to have the provinces determine the point at which bilingual court facilities can be established. Both these amendments indicate an understanding on the part of the national government of the problems facing certain provinces in implementing fully the terms of the official languages bill. Often we hear it said that the problems in the maritimes should be given a greater measure of understanding. It is said that Quebec has problems not appreciated by all of us. The same claim may be made with respect to Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Often the west is portrayed as an area peopled by intransigent, inflexible Canadians enjoying above average incomes in some areas and a below average comprehension of questions relating to national unity. As a westerner this diagnosis represents a vast oversimplification and is not fair to the people living in western Canada.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I ask for understanding for my province of British Columbia. If we are not as bilingual and bicultural as some other provinces, it is because long ago when people first saw the possibility of settlement in our province relatively few people of French language and culture came to help us settle the province. Those who did come made a fine contribution and have maintained significantly their French language and cultural rights, at the same time contributing richly to the development of our economy in British Columbia. When our institutions were being shaped,
May 21, 1969

formed and developed, few from the French area of Canada were there to help.
We developed a multicultural province. Settling of the province was accomplished by the English, Scots, Irish, Welsh, Americans, Ukrainians, Chinese, Japanese, Germans, Italians, Hungarians, Scandinavians and people from many other lands, but very few French. So if we in British Columbia appear to be bewildered at times about the bilingualism dialogue, at least part of the fault must be laid at the doorstep of the leaders of French Canada historically, who many years ago determined to concentrate on a program of developing primarily within the boundaries of one province their language and cultural institutions. I suggest it is unfair to say to British Columbians that they should get with it and appreciate a dialogue that most of them thought was confined to the St. Lawrence river valley. Perhaps in the context of this historical fact the attitude of British Columbians and many other western Canadians can be understood.
We are as interested in national unity as anyone living in Ontario, the maritimes or Quebec. But we have developed and grown in a different way. We have had people of all races and religions come to the province. It is an area remarkably free of prejudice of any kind. I am proud of the west and I do not like some of the cynical editorials that we see written in eastern Canada which suggest that somehow western Canadians belong in the neanderthal age because they do not fully agree with all the policies that are advanced in other parts of Canada.
The amendments recognize-and this is why I welcome them-the unique evolution of the western provinces. In this sense the amendments are conciliatory and very useful, and I hope they will be welcomed by the people of my province.
As we move to send the bill to a special committee we should remember that only a year ago the Prime Minister travelled to every part of Canada with one message which he delivered in both French and English. He expressed his views on language rights and spoke of them in the campaign everywhere he went, from one end of Canada to the other. Speaking in both languages, he spoke of the need for guaranteeing to each language group the right to the protection and preservation of both languages. He was acclaimed and applauded, and significantly was elected with a substantial majority.
Official Languages
We now have the proposed legislation before us. With its amendments I believe it gives expression to the aspirations of most Canadians in most provinces. Happily it enjoys the support of most members of all parties in this house. This is not the time for hesitation, for criticism and backbiting; this is the time to give the bill second reading, approval in principle. Let us send it to the committee and make certain that it is the best possible legislation that can be produced at this time. Let members of all parties in the house make constructive contributions at the committee stage. It will then be time to approve the bill, either as it is or as amended, to implement it, and then get on with the job of moving on to other trouble spots in this country.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak cm this measure I suggest that this language bill is a conglomerate of administrative decisions compounded by constitutional infringement. To legislate on language rights is a direct intrusion into an area reserved for constitutional enactment.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) knows that the only way he can validly proceed is to bring the matter before the constitutional conference and seek the consent of the provinces to amend the constitution. Since a constitutional conference will shortly be convening this would be an ideal time. Instead, he seeks to do by the back door what he dare not do by the front door. If this government, by a simple majority, can produce a constitutional change in an area so basic as language rights, there is no area of the constitution that they cannot deal with. To legislate the equality of both languages on an official basis is, of course, itself a constitutional amendment. The only real and effective guarantee of equality must be embedded in the constitution.
According to section 91(1) of the British North America Act, which was inserted by the St. Laurent government in 1949, parliament is prohibited from unilaterally legislating in the language field. This is, of course, the reason we have a constitution, so that those things inserted therein are accorded a degree of protection.
Now the Prime Minister has made the constitution a dead letter. He is driving a truck through Canada's constitution, simply treating it as though it did not exist. What one government can do, another government can do.

May 21, 1969
Official Languages
If constitutional prerogatives are to be treated with disdain, what is to prevent a government from altering the whole basis of educational rights simply by passing a bill in parliament? Then a following government could wipe out this provision by simply repealing it.
There are a number of questions which must be asked in regard to the bill itself. What does it seek to accomplish, and how successful is it in so doing? With regard to the use of the French language in parliament, that is already recognized. The use of French in the civil service was already announced as the policy of the Pearson government. This bill goes farther and translates into legislation what was previously announced as policy. Obviously the intention is that Canada shall become officially a bilingual nation with both languages granted equal status.
What about the bilingual districts? This is a new departure and one cannot be sure at this stage whether it is a wise one. As has already been stated, there is a danger of the bilingual districts becoming bilingual ghettos and of services provided there being denied elsewhere. This is a problem for the government.
What about industry? Will industry going into a district designated as a bilingual district be expected to observe that designation in its personnel policy? Will it be discreetly pointed out that an industry wishing to establish itself in a bilingual district and seek the benefit of area development assistance will be expected to conform to the bilingual character of the district? Is this to be part of the policy?
There are many other unanswered questions about bilingual districts. On what basis will they be set up? Can a minority of 100 in a block be expanded to include 900 of the majority in order to dilute the original ratio to 10 per cent? Can a minority of 1,000 be expanded to include 9,000 of the majority? Especially in rural areas this might mean that people living miles from the minority are included in the majority. If people in a bilingual district are entitled to service in their mother tongue at the federal level, they need it much more at the provincial and municipal level. If one area of government is bilingual at the federal level, how much more important that the lower levels are also bilingual. A citizen would be able to pay local taxes, converse with the dog tax licence bureau, do business with the income tax inspector, the unemployment insurance official and with the R.C.M.P. Indeed this would be a good way to

deal with speeding tickets. An army of people will be required to carry out even rudimentary government.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Other questions are being asked. Will bilingual districts be able to dissolve? There is no indication this will be possible. How will the criteria of a bilingual district be arrived at? Presumably the census-taker will decide the mother tongue of the citizen. Will it be the citizen's right to change this? Many citizens change their mother tongue in the midstream of life in a practical way. They start to think in the second language. There has been no definition of a mother tongue.
In a practical way it seems that the bilingual districts will be largely rural. Without the co-operation of the provincial governments, bilingual districts will not be carried forward without language education. Sociologists say that as well as being a poverty creator rural backwardness is largely educational. Will the resources be available to keep the extra educational facilities on an equal level with the neighbouring unilingual districts? In fact the bilingual rural districts will almost certainly be deprived areas.
What about the provinces? What is the situation when the federal government says to a province, we are setting up a number of bilingual districts in this province? What is the position of the provincial government? Surely language is a civil right under the jurisdiction of a province. Is there not going to be some degree of consultation with the province? What if the province's views on what constitutes a bilingual district differs from the views of the federal government?
These are some of the aspects which the government should have carefully studied before presenting this biE, rather than simply accepting the recommendations of the B and B Commission as though they were written on tablets of stone. If the bilingual districts become a bone of contention between the federal government and any or all provinces, surely this legislation will set back the cause of bilingualism rather than advancing it. We must carefully scrutinize the basic question of bilingualism in this country and view this bill in the light of the requirements of national unity.
Obviously the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is endeavouring to bring about a situation where he can point to the official equality of both languages from coast to coast as a counter to those who would separate Quebec
May 21, 1969

from the rest of Canada, partly on grounds of failure to recognize the language and culture of Quebec outside of that province. The question is whether this bill brings about such a situation effectively. In short, will it satisfy Mr. Levesque? Obviously the answer is no.
Presumably in setting up bilingual districts the Prime Minister has in mind seeking the consent of the provinces for setting up schools in both languages within those bilingual districts. This, of course, could only be done by agreement, and would in all likelihood require a constitutional amendment. It is reasonable that the enunciation of so basic a right should be inscribed in the constitution rather than simply by way of parliamentary enactment.
The real issues are recognition of both languages from coast to coast and education in both languages where warranted by demand. What is required is agreement on constitutional changes. The present bill, in so far as it seeks to accomplish what the Prime Minister knows is fundamental to the problem, is really little more than a declaration of intention. I venture to suggest this because we have been going at the problem the wrong way. Surely the place to start is with the prior consent of the provinces, through consultation and agreement. For some reason it has been very difficult to get the present government and its predecessor to see the necessity of the principle of prior consultation. Once it is accepted, I am sure we can begin to bring order out of chaos.
In essence the bill confirms what is already laid down in the B.N.A. Act with regard to the federal parliament and courts. It breaks new ground in the enactment in statutory form of the policy of bilingualism in the civil service, the provision of bilingual districts and the creation of the office of commissioner of official languages, who may hereinafter be referred to as the bilingual watchdog. Apparently he will be a sort of Auditor General of bilingualism. One hopes he will have more success in getting his recommendations adopted than the Auditor General has had with this government and its predecessor. The only thing that seems to be missing from the comprehensive description of the language commissioner's office and duties is the requirement that he and every member of his staff be bilingual.
This bill effectively rules that the whole of the civil service must be bilingual. This will include all the crown corporations. It is fine to say that merit will be the deciding factor,
Official Languages
but when hiring new employees merit is of no value because it cannot be assessed. When an official is hiring new civil servants, bilingualism will be the first requirement. The officials cannot go wrong if he hires a bilingual person. However, he can go wrong when hiring a unilingual person no matter how great and merit-worthy that person may be.
To succeed in the civil service, bilingualism will be necessary. Crown corporations will be composed largely of French speaking personnel. There is no doubt that in the foreseeable future the majority of the business in Canada will be conducted in the English language, while civil service functions will largely be conducted by those with a French background. This will cause considerable inefficiency and probably duplication. Most French speaking Canadians will necessarily be recruited in the province of Quebec. As they move to other parts of Canada their French background may be lost within a generation.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
To my knowledge, no country other than Belgium has attempted on a massive scale to have a bilingual population. There are nations such as Russia that have many languages but have remained with one official language. The people of India are struggling with this very same problem. Until now they have been using English, but they have finally decided upon one of their own languages and they intend to impose it as best they can upon the whole of that country.
We cannot live alone. If bilingualism is to be carried forward, surely it will truly embody the idea that French and English will be equally available throughout Canada at the federal level, and it also implies that services in these languages should be available at the provincial and municipal levels. Whether or not the country can afford this remains to be seen.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept the principle of two founding nations and the proposals contained in this bill. I believe that all the premiers of Canada and the majority of Canadians accept the principle of equality of English and French, and that the only real difference between us is by what manner and how quickly implementing procedures can be adopted to bring about our objective in the fairest and most effective manner.
As has been pointed out, the bill will raise some problems in administration but all these can and must be solved. But before we look

May 21. 1969
Official Languages
at them I wish to mention some of the positive aspects of this legislation so that we may weigh them against the effort required to accomplish the desired result.
What are some of the good things that the bill will do for Canada? It will promote among all French speaking and all English speaking Canadians a feeling of equality. It will improve and increase the mobility of these Canadians in all parts of Canada. It will open up opportunity for many, particularly of the younger generation, to enjoy two cultures and thus share more fully in the Canadian community. It will give Canadians an international image of bilingualism, good will and co-operation. It will carry out the will of certainly the majority of Canadians as expressed in the last election. Above all, without it we cannot maintain unity, or perhaps even long remain as Canadians. It is as simple as that.
Because the philosophy of the bill deals with fundamental human rights it has a status comparable to a constitutional document. Some will argue that the goal can be reached voluntarily and that legislation is not necessary. I cannot agree. At times and in certain places some would allow their personal views and prejudices to overcome the spirit of the principle, and this in turn could stimulate reciprocal intolerances and resentment. For that reason I think it better that the detail be spelled out in legislation so that the courts, the commissioner to be appointed pursuant to the bill, and all others know clearly the intention of parliament. This is not a time for loose ends.
But clause 11 bothers me. There are some wrinkles which require ironing out to prevent confusion in future. Clause 11(2) provides that in every federal court of record-Exchequer, Admiralty and Bankruptcy-held in the national capital region or in a federal bilingual district there is to be simultaneous translation, except where this service cannot be conveniently provided and a party would not be put at a disadvantage.
Clause 11(3) provides that in any criminal court-Magistrates Court, County Court Judge's Criminal Court, Supreme Court or Court of Appeal-the court may at the request of the accused order the proceedings to be held completely in one of the two languages. This would apply to the federal bilingual districts only. This discretionary power in the courts, however, does not apply to subclause (1).
Clause 11(1) provides that in every federal court or administrative tribunal and in every

criminal court in Canada, as distinguished from those in bilingual districts only, the court must ensure that any person appearing and giving evidence before it may be heard in the official language of his choice, and that in being so heard he will not be placed at a disadvantage because he does not know the other official language.
This means that an accused or his counsel in being heard can plead, argue, address the court or jury, examine or cross-examine in the language of his choice, and this could take place in any part of Canada. There is no power in the court to relieve, as under subclauses (2) and (3). Certainly this is the ideal and must eventually come because anything less does not create equality. But apparently there were objections, probably based on the lack of bilingual lawyers and other bilingual personnel in the non-bilingual districts. The proposed amendment, tabled on May 20, changes the wording of this subclause to read:
Any person giving evidence before such court may be heard in the official language of his choice.
This is probably meant to apply to his role as a witness only. But if so it is not necessary. Every Canadian already has the right to give evidence in the language of his choice through an interpreter in a criminal proceeding, and this is guaranteed by the Bill of Rights.
Dealing with the wording of the proposed amendment I point out that if an accused as a witness is heard in the language of his choice while giving his evidence, surely the court is bound to hear him in argument and in crossexamination in the same language. If so the desired change will not be accomplished. Rather than "heard" it would be better to say "he may give such evidence". Such an amendment could very well avoid an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada and a long period of uncertainty. As an alternative we could leave the clause as it is but make it applicable to the national capital region and the bilingual districts only. This I prefer because it would be relatively simple to provide this right in the bilingual districts where there is simultaneous translation.
I agree that there will be problems, for example in jury trials. But these problems have been overcome in Quebec, India, South Africa, Finland, Switzerland and other countries. It is no answer to say that in some parts of the country the percentage is not large enough. Once we adopt the equality of the two languages it must be as universal as
May 21, 1969	COMMONS
reasonably possible. With a bilingual bar we could overcome the difficulty almost immediately. Lawyers, next to politicians, will be involved the most, and to them will fall the opportunity to make a tremendous contribution to the success of this measure.
There are solutions available. What is to prevent reciprocal bar privileges and an exchange of students between bilingual provinces and the other provinces? Why can some of their instruction not be in the second language as is the case with many other students across Canada? Quebec and New Brunswick could export or lend us bilingual lawyers pending the development of our own.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Why could this bill not cover drafting as well? In Canada drafting is done in English and then it is translated into French. The preparation of important legislation should not involve the translation from one language to the other. The approach to legislation involving two languages and two cultures must be from a dynamic and not merely a mechanical point of view. Both should be drafted together as is the case in Switzerland. When they have a word there which cannot be translated they send it back to the legislative committee with the suggestion that
DEBATES	8927
Official Languages
another word which can be translated into their official languages be used. I suggest it is imperative that this type of drafting be commenced immediately. To save the expense of redrafting legislation in both languages in the nine common law provinces, uniformity in legislation should be encouraged. We should also push ahead with an agreed upon French-English dictionary for legislative purposes as has been done in Belgium. In Canada we are behind. We do not even have agreement among the universities concerning the acceptance of an English-French dictionary.
In conclusion may I say that I hope for speedy conclusion of this debate so that we may get on with the details in the committee as soon as possible.
